title: Stoic in illness
hook: the leg is hindered, not the will

segments.voice: Yesterday: Stoic in anger, the jolt, the delay and the other handle. Your line was delay the reply. Did a message test you, and did you wait? Day six hundred eighty-one.

Day three of the flu. The ceiling has become very familiar. The to-do list on your phone looks like a message from another planet. You feel useless, and then guilty for feeling useless, and then annoyed at yourself for feeling guilty. Or maybe it's not three days. Maybe it's a back that hasn't worked right for years, or an illness that comes and goes on its own schedule. Epictetus walked with a limp his whole adult life, and Seneca was sick for much of his. They both wrote about it, from the inside. Today: Stoic in illness.
screen: `DAY THREE OF THE FLU.` → `USELESS, THEN GUILTY.` → `WRITTEN FROM THE INSIDE.`

segments.voice: First, Epictetus's line. In the Handbook, section nine: illness is a hindrance to the body, but not to the will, unless the will itself chooses it. Lameness hinders the leg, not the will. Say that to yourself, he says, about everything that happens, and you'll find it hinders something else, but not you. Remember who's saying it: a man who limped, probably his whole life. Second, the Greek word for will. Prohairesis: the faculty of choosing, your power to judge, decide and respond. For Epictetus it's the part of you that's most truly yours. A fever can take your energy, your plans, your week. It can't make your choices for you. You can still choose patience, honesty, gratitude to whoever brings the soup. Third, Seneca's honesty. In one letter he admits that as a young man he was so sick, for so long, that he came close to despair. What held him, he says, was his friends, and his studies. He also notes that illness brings three burdens: fear, pain, and losing your usual pleasures. He doesn't pretend they're nothing. He just refuses to let them be everything. Fourth, kindness to the body. Being Stoic in illness doesn't mean pushing through or skipping the doctor. The body is not up to you in the end, but caring for it is. Rest, fluids, medicine, a day off without guilt: those are wise choices, made by a will that isn't sick. The leg is hindered. The will can still choose to be gentle with the leg.
screen: `THE LEG IS HINDERED, NOT THE WILL.` · `PROHAIRESIS: YOUR POWER TO CHOOSE.` · `SENECA: FRIENDS AND STUDIES HELD ME.` · `GENTLE WITH THE BODY.` · then, large: `NOT THE WILL.`

segments.voice: Settle into a comfortable position, whatever that means for your body today. Scan slowly from head to feet. Where is there pain, tiredness, stiffness? Don't fight it. Just name it: this is the body. Now notice the part of you that's noticing, the part that chooses how to meet it. Say silently, the body is hindered, not the will. Then ask the will one kind question: what does this body need from me today? The bell holds the time.
Stoic in illness: the body may be hindered, but the will, your power to choose, is still yours, and it can choose rest and kindness. Today's word.
Your line: not the will. Do one kind thing for your body today, rest, water, a walk or a doctor's appointment you've been putting off. Day six hundred eighty-one.

howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners meet illness by separating what the body suffers from how they choose to respond, while still resting and seeking medical care.

what it means: the body is hindered, the will isn't, and the will can choose rest, care and patience.
what a scholar hears: Handbook 9 says illness is an impediment to the body, not to prohairesis; ancient sources differ on how Epictetus became lame; Seneca's Letters 78 recounts his youthful illness.

notes: Epictetus's lameness: sources differ (from birth, rheumatism, or a master's cruelty per Celsus via Origen); script says 'probably his whole life'. Confirm wording.

Letters 78 paraphrased: youthful illness, thoughts of ending his life held back by his father (omitted here), comfort from friends and studies; three burdens of illness: fear of death, bodily pain, interruption of pleasures. Confirm.
